title: When Is Personalized Federated Learning Worth Its Deployment Cost?

paper.title: When Is Personalized Federated Learning Worth Its Deployment Cost?
paper.abstract: Abstract Personalized federated learning (PFL) may improve client-level performance, but deeper personalization increases deployment cost. We formulate personalization-depth selection as a utility-based empirical decision problem in which client utility equals Macro-F1 minus a cost-sensitivity weight times deployment cost, over six personalization depths labeled P0 through P5. We compare fixed policies with an offline per-client Oracle reference and report allocation maps over Dirichlet data heterogeneity and cost sensitivity. Although evaluated on this hierarchy, the formulation can accommodate any finite candidate set. On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and a PTB-XL subset, personalization shows empirical, setting-dependent decision regimes rather than a universal benefit: higher cost sensitivity shifts Oracle mass toward the global-only depth P0; low cost sensitivity can favor deeper actions. Patterns are grid observations (three seeds per cell), not theoretical boundaries. Best-uniform is competitive with Oracle assignment (6.5 percent plus or minus 7.8 percent relative regret; 95 percent confidence interval 5.9 to 7.1), whereas random and personalize-all incur much larger regret (189.3 percent plus or minus 367.1 percent and 409.0 percent plus or minus 803.2 percent). Under the same utility, Ditto full-model personalization is substantially suboptimal once cost is counted. The contribution is an offline characterization of when personalization depth is worth its cost, not a new PFL optimizer or deployment-time scheduler.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Federated learning (FL) trains models across decentralized clients without pooling raw data. Personalized FL (PFL) adapts models to client-specific distributions through fine-tuning, regularization, representation sharing, or client-specific layers [ 10 , 11 ] . Most PFL work therefore asks how to personalize. Deployment raises a complementary question: when is personalization worth its deployment cost? Personalization consumes computation, parameters, memory, communication, and operational complexity. Personalizing every client may waste resources when the global model already suffices; a global-only policy may fail for strongly heterogeneous clients. We present a utility-based empirical decision framework for personalization-depth selection: measure predictive performance and deployment cost, form a performance–cost utility, obtain an offline Oracle reference by ex-post argmax over a finite action set, and characterize regret of practical uniform policies. Experiments instantiate 𝒜 = { P 0 , … , P 5 } \mathcal{A}=\{P_{0},\ldots,P_{5}\} and compare global-only, best-uniform, random, personalize-all, and Ditto against that Oracle. This is not a new PFL optimizer, not a deployment-time scheduler, and not a universal theory of personalization. Contributions: (i) we formulate personalization-depth selection as a finite performance–cost utility-maximization problem; (ii) we instantiate the decision space with the six-level P 0 P_{0} – P 5 P_{5} hierarchy and characterize offline Oracle assignments across heterogeneity and cost-sensitivity regimes; (iii) we quantify regret of deployable uniform policies relative to the Oracle reference and identify empirical decision regimes in which deeper personalization is or is not worth its cost; and (iv) we note that the formulation is action-space agnostic while limiting empirical claims to the evaluated P 0 P_{0} – P 5 P_{5} setting (including a PTB-XL subset and Ditto under the same utility).

sections.heading: II-A Classical Federated Learning
sections.text: FedAvg [ 1 ] learns a shared global model. FedProx [ 2 ] , SCAFFOLD [ 3 ] , FedNova [ 4 ] , and adaptive server optimization [ 5 ] address heterogeneity. Surveys document open problems and scale [ 6 , 7 ] . Non-IID effects have been measured directly [ 8 , 9 ] .

sections.heading: II-B Personalized FL: How to Personalize
sections.text: The PerFedAvg method [ 10 ] uses meta-learning; Ditto [ 11 ] and pFedMe [ 12 ] regularize personalized objectives. FedPer [ 13 ] personalizes classifier heads; FedRep [ 14 ] separates representation and classifier. FedBN [ 18 ] uses local batch normalization for feature shift; FedBABU [ 15 ] decouples body and head training; APFL [ 16 ] adaptively mixes global and local models; and FedAMP [ 17 ] clusters similar clients. Adapters appear in pFedLoRA [ 19 ] , following LoRA [ 20 ] . FedALA [ 21 ] and personalization-layer decoupling [ 22 ] refine client capacity. Peer-reviewed 2025 methods continue this axis: FedFSA [ 23 ] and PFedCS [ 24 ] . Large-model personalization includes FLoRA [ 25 ] and OpenFedLLM [ 26 ] . Surveys catalogue many “how” methods [ 35 ] . Deployment cost rarely enters as an explicit shared utility over personalization depth.

sections.heading: II-C This Work: When Personalization Is Worth Its Cost
sections.text: We ask under which ( task , α , λ ) (\text{task},\alpha,\lambda) client i i should personalize, and to what depth. Rather than proposing another PFL trainer or online allocator, we evaluate fixed policies, an offline Oracle reference, and Ditto under ( 2 ), map empirical decision regimes over ( α , λ ) (\alpha,\lambda) , and report regret with confidence intervals.

sections.heading: II-D Resource-Aware FL and Benchmarks
sections.text: Resource-aware FL uses local SGD [ 27 ] , quantization [ 28 ] , compression [ 29 ] , and client selection such as FedCS [ 30 ] , Oort [ 31 ] , and TiFL [ 32 ] . HeteroFL [ 33 ] trains heterogeneous local capacities toward one global model; related personalized communication-efficient designs appear in industrial IoT [ 34 ] . Hardware-aware FL further couples client selection and local workload to device profiles under communication and latency constraints [ 42 ] . Benchmarks include LEAF [ 36 ] , FedScale [ 37 ] , FedML [ 38 ] , FLamby [ 39 ] , and PTB-XL [ 40 ] ; multi-institutional ECG FL has also been studied under encryption-based privacy constraints [ 41 ] .

sections.heading: III Formulation and Experimental Design
sections.text: Clients i ∈ { 1 , … , N } i\in\{1,\ldots,N\} participate in FedAvg [ 1 ] to obtain a global model, then apply a client-specific personalization action on held-out data.

sections.heading: Decision Formulation.
sections.text: We formulate personalization-depth selection as a finite utility-maximization problem. The decision maker is a system designer, deployment planner, or FL practitioner selecting a personalization strategy under a specified performance–cost preference. The decision variable is an action a ∈ 𝒜 a\in\mathcal{A} . In our experiments the finite action space is the six-level personalization hierarchy adopted in this study, 𝒜 = { P 0 , P 1 , P 2 , P 3 , P 4 , P 5 } , \mathcal{A}=\{P_{0},P_{1},P_{2},P_{3},P_{4},P_{5}\}, (1) (Table I ): an ordered operationalization of personalization depth for controlled analysis, not a universal taxonomy or the complete space of PFL strategies. For client i i , utility is U i ​ ( a ) = Macro ​ - ​ F1 i ​ ( a ) − λ ​ Cost i ​ ( a ) , U_{i}(a)=\mathrm{Macro\text{-}F1}_{i}(a)-\lambda\,\mathrm{Cost}_{i}(a), (2) where Macro ​ - ​ F1 i ​ ( a ) \mathrm{Macro\text{-}F1}_{i}(a) is predictive performance, Cost i ​ ( a ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \mathrm{Cost}_{i}(a)\in[0,1] is the normalized deployment-cost proxy (Section III-A ), and λ ≥ 0 \lambda\geq 0 is the cost-sensitivity preference. The preferred action is a i ⋆ = arg ⁡ max a ∈ 𝒜 ​ U i ​ ( a ) . a_{i}^{\star}=\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}U_{i}(a). (3) Scope conditions only: a a must belong to the evaluated set 𝒜 \mathcal{A} ; performance and cost must be measurable or estimable; the cost model and λ \lambda are specified before utility comparison; and the Oracle reference is restricted to evaluated candidates. This specifies the decision problem and its empirical reference solution; it does not constitute a deployment-time policy. The linear utility is intentionally a transparent first-order approximation. It provides an interpretable performance–cost trade-off through a single parameter λ \lambda under a constant marginal cost penalty, while avoiding deployment-specific nonlinear assumptions that cannot be justified uniformly across heterogeneous platforms. Nonlinear, thresholded, or hardware-specific utilities may be appropriate elsewhere.

sections.heading: Role of the Oracle.
sections.text: The Oracle is an offline, ex-post reference rule that selects the utility-maximizing action after all candidate actions have been evaluated ( 3 ). It is an empirical upper-bound reference over measured utilities in 𝒜 \mathcal{A} : it is not deployable, not predictive, does not generate utility values, does not possess future information, does not avoid exhaustive evaluation, and is not an online scheduler. Methodological pipeline: measure predictive performance; estimate deployment cost; compute U i ​ ( a ) U_{i}(a) ; select a i ⋆ a_{i}^{\star} with the offline Oracle; compute regret r i ​ ( π ) = U i ​ ( a i ⋆ ) − U i ​ ( π i ) r_{i}(\pi)=U_{i}(a_{i}^{\star})-U_{i}(\pi_{i}) as a downstream evaluation measure; then analyze the decision landscape. We report mean regret, relative regret r ¯ rel = r ¯ / max ⁡ ( | U ¯ ​ ( Oracle ) | , ϵ ) \bar{r}_{\mathrm{rel}}=\bar{r}/\max(|\bar{U}(\textsc{Oracle})|,\epsilon) , and Oracle win rate over ( α , λ ) (\alpha,\lambda) [ 8 ] via P0 ratio, deep ratio ( P 3 P_{3} – P 5 P_{5} ), and gaps to fixed baselines.

sections.heading: Generality of the Oracle Framework.
sections.text: Although instantiated with P 0 P_{0} – P 5 P_{5} , the formulation is agnostic to the semantic meaning of candidate actions. More generally, 𝒜 \mathcal{A} may contain any finite set of personalization or deployment alternatives—adapter configurations, LoRA ranks, alternative PFL methods, model-compression choices, or edge–cloud execution modes. The offline Oracle requires only measured utilities and selects their argmax. The generality is methodological rather than empirical: the present experiments validate the formulation only for the P 0 P_{0} – P 5 P_{5} action space considered in this work. sections.heading: Why this hierarchy?
sections.text: 𝒜 \mathcal{A} is a practical discretization spanning global-only inference to full local fine-tuning by progressively increasing trainable client-specific components; it does not exhaust every PFL design. Cost generally increases with depth by construction; predictive performance and utility need not increase monotonically. P 0 P_{0} is FedAvg [ 1 ] ; P 1 P_{1} mirrors head-only personalization [ 13 ] ; P 2 P_{2} adds an adapter plus head [ 20 , 19 ] ; P 3 P_{3} – P 4 P_{4} unfreeze last encoder block(s) [ 14 ] ; P 5 P_{5} is full-model fine-tuning (Ditto cost extremity [ 11 ] ). Six ordered depths resolve empirical regime-change patterns without enumerating every layer mask.

sections.heading: Datasets and protocol.
sections.text: Experiments use CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, an auxiliary CIFAR-10 vision split, and a PTB-XL subset for binary ECG classification [ 40 ] . The subset uses Lead II only, the WFDB records100 release at 100 Hz, at most 5000 records, and a binary Normal vs. Abnormal label derived from SCP-ECG codes. Unlike privacy-preserving multi-institutional ECG FL with homomorphic encryption [ 41 ] , our ECG evaluation is a cost-aware personalization-depth study on a public PTB-XL subset rather than a clinical deployment system. We run FedAvg for 5 global rounds and 3 local epochs, then evaluate all actions in 𝒜 \mathcal{A} on held-out data. Client-level metrics are computed for each ( dataset , seed , α , N ) (\text{dataset},\text{seed},\alpha,N) configuration; λ \lambda sweeps are applied post hoc. Allocation map: 378 cells (3 datasets × \times 7 α \alpha × \times 6 λ \lambda × \times 3 seeds), α ∈ { 0.01 , 0.05 , 0.1 , 0.3 , 0.5 , 1.0 , 10.0 } \alpha\in\{0.01,0.05,0.1,0.3,0.5,1.0,10.0\} , λ ∈ { 0 , 0.1 , 0.3 , 0.5 , 1.0 , 2.0 } \lambda\in\{0,0.1,0.3,0.5,1.0,2.0\} , 20 clients. Sparsity validation: 54 cells (3 datasets × \times 3 α \alpha × \times 3 seeds × \times 2 client counts), α ∈ { 0.1 , 0.5 , 1.0 } \alpha\in\{0.1,0.5,1.0\} . Regret study: 594 cells (99 configurations × \times 6 λ \lambda × \times 5 policies). Ditto [ 11 ] is scored with P5-equivalent cost. Image tasks use a ResNet-style encoder; ECG uses a 1D ResNet on Lead II (1000 samples, per-lead z-score). Dirichlet client splits use 70/15/15 train/val/test.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: The global-only policy uses P 0 P_{0} for all clients; the personalize-all policy uses P 5 P_{5} for all; the random policy samples depths without utility awareness; and the best-uniform policy chooses the best single depth for all clients within a configuration. The best-uniform policy is intentionally strong because it represents a realistic low-complexity deployment alternative to heterogeneous per-client allocation.

sections.heading: III-B Evaluation Protocol
sections.text: All policies share the same client partitions and held-out splits. After FedAvg, each personalization action in 𝒜 \mathcal{A} is evaluated locally. Regret against the best-uniform policy measures how much utility practical uniform selection loses relative to client-specific offline Oracle assignments. We report mean ± \pm std and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (10,000 resamples) over cells; Student’s t t and bootstrap intervals agree closely for best-uniform regret ( t t -CI [ 5.86 , 7.12 ] [5.86,7.12] , bootstrap [ 5.89 , 7.15 ] [5.89,7.15] ). Paired Wilcoxon tests (Table IX ) are descriptive (no family-wise correction).

sections.heading: IV-A Finding 1: Empirical regime-change patterns
sections.text: Fig. 1 shows that offline Oracle assignment changes sharply over the ( α , λ ) (\alpha,\lambda) grid. As λ \lambda increases, mass shifts toward P 0 P_{0} because marginal Macro-F1 gain no longer offsets deployment cost; at low λ \lambda , deeper actions P 3 P_{3} – P 5 P_{5} reappear where client data are sufficiently heterogeneous. We describe these as empirical regime-change patterns on a finite three-seed grid—not theoretically derived phase transitions. Observed boundaries depend on datasets, architectures, seeds, heterogeneity, cost normalization, λ \lambda , and the P 0 P_{0} – P 5 P_{5} action space. The pattern appears across modalities but occupies different heatmap regions. sections.heading: V Statistical Validation

sections.heading: Accuracy-only evaluation is incomplete.
sections.text: At λ = 0 \lambda{=}0 , the offline Oracle selects deep personalization in isolated cells. Claims about sparsity or depth must specify ( U , λ ) (U,\lambda) ; accuracy-only plots can overstate deep personalization and understate global-only efficiency when λ > 0 \lambda{>}0 .

sections.heading: Best-uniform policy as deployment benchmark.
sections.text: As reported in Finding 2, the best-uniform policy is competitive across many configurations. Deployment systems should report regret against this policy before adopting heterogeneous allocation.

sections.heading: Objectives can diverge.
sections.text: Ditto results illustrate that accuracy-oriented and deployment-aware utilities may favor different operating points: full-model personalization is penalized under U U when marginal Macro-F1 gain does not offset full-depth cost.

sections.heading: Allocation maps as reporting practice.
sections.text: We advocate utility curves over λ \lambda , P0/deep ratios, and regret versus fixed policies with uncertainty bands—shifting from “does personalization improve accuracy?” to “under which ( task , α , λ ) (\text{task},\alpha,\lambda) is it worth its deployment cost?” Table X lists minimum reporting items.

sections.heading: Decision formulation vs. decision policy.
sections.text: The framework separates decision formulation from decision policy. This study addresses the former by defining candidate actions, the utility objective, and an offline Oracle reference, and by empirically characterizing the resulting decision landscape. It does not provide a deployment-time policy that selects an action without evaluating alternatives. The characterization may support subsequent lightweight rules, calibration procedures, learned policies, or adaptive schedulers, but such mechanisms remain outside the present scope.

sections.heading: Practical offline calibration.
sections.text: Exhaustive P 0 P_{0} – P 5 P_{5} evaluation is intended for offline characterization rather than routine deployment. In practice, a system designer could apply the framework during a calibration or pilot phase on representative clients, identify which actions dominate under relevant heterogeneity and cost regimes, and use the resulting evidence to define a simpler deployment policy. Recalibration may be needed if the architecture, client population, hardware, cost model, or λ \lambda range changes. Migrating from synthetic to real WFDB ECG lowered P0 ratio from 81.6% to 0.552 ± 0.167 0.552\pm 0.167 at λ = 0.3 \lambda{=}0.3 , illustrating that modality choice can shift observed regimes.

sections.heading: Formulation-level generality vs. experiment-level scope.
sections.text: The same decision rule can, in principle, apply to other finite sets after redefining 𝒜 \mathcal{A} and the cost model. Generality claimed here is methodological rather than empirical: experiments validate only the P 0 P_{0} – P 5 P_{5} hierarchy. TABLE X: RECOMMENDED REPORTING ITEMS FOR UTILITY-AWARE PFL EVALUATION. sections.heading: VII Limitations
sections.text: While the decision formulation accommodates arbitrary finite candidate sets, the present empirical findings are specific to the evaluated P 0 P_{0} – P 5 P_{5} hierarchy, datasets, architectures, heterogeneity settings, cost normalization, default weights, and λ \lambda range. We therefore do not claim that observed Oracle frequencies, regret values, or regime boundaries transfer unchanged to alternative PFL methods or deployment environments. The cost model is a normalized proxy rather than real-device measurement; λ \lambda is a preference parameter, not a universally identifiable constant. The offline Oracle cannot be used directly during deployment. PTB-XL evidence is intentionally narrower than CIFAR (Lead II subset, ≤ \leq 5000 records, binary labels) and does not substitute for broader clinical evaluation. Additional limits: three seeds, simulated hardware multipliers, no native FEMNIST, one PFL comparator (Ditto), and uncorrected descriptive Wilcoxon tests. Future work includes alternative action spaces, real-device measurements, additional medical datasets, application-specific costs, and lightweight deployment policies derived from offline calibration.

sections.heading: VIII Conclusion
sections.text: Personalization value in federated learning is regime-dependent rather than universal. Under U = Performance − λ ⋅ Cost U=\mathrm{Performance}-\lambda\cdot\mathrm{Cost} with default weighting and 𝒜 = { P 0 , … , P 5 } \mathcal{A}=\{P_{0},\ldots,P_{5}\} , offline Oracle depth varies with dataset, α \alpha , and λ \lambda . High λ \lambda concentrates mass on P 0 P_{0} on several vision tasks; low λ \lambda restores deeper personalization; modality shifts empirical regimes. Best-uniform remains close ( 6.5 % ± 7.8 % 6.5\%\pm 7.8\% ; CI [ 5.9 , 7.1 ] [5.9,7.1] ; 82.5% win rate); personalize-all and random do not. At λ = 0.3 \lambda{=}0.3 , mean P0 ratio 0.499 ± 0.317 0.499\pm 0.317 rejects universal global-only and universal deep-personalization laws. This work does not propose a deployment-time personalization algorithm. Instead, it formulates personalization-depth selection as a utility-based empirical decision problem and characterizes its offline decision landscape using an Oracle reference. The resulting evidence can inform future calibration rules or lightweight deployment policies, whose design and validation remain outside the present scope, including alternative PFL methods, parameter-efficient adaptation, real-device measurements, additional medical datasets, and application-specific cost functions.

sections.heading: Impact Statement
sections.text: This work analyzes resource–accuracy trade-offs using public CIFAR and PTB-XL releases; all datasets used in this study are publicly available, and no new patient-identifiable data are collected. Source code is available at https://github.com/bbyuksel .

Beyazıt Bestami Yüksel Affiliation: Computer Engineering Istanbul Technical University Istanbul, Türkiye yukselbe18@itu.edu.tr Ayşe Yılmazer Metin Affiliation: Computer Engineering Istanbul Technical University Istanbul, Türkiye yilmazerayse@itu.edu.tr Emrah Dikbıyık Affiliation: Computer Engineering Marmara University Istanbul, Türkiye emrah.dikbiyik@marmara.edu.tr Abstract Personalized federated learning (PFL) may improve client-level performance, but deeper personalization increases deployment cost. We formulate personalization-depth selection as a utility-based empirical decision problem in which client utility equals Macro-F1 minus a cost-sensitivity weight times deployment cost, over six personalization depths labeled P0 through P5. We compare fixed policies with an offline per-client Oracle reference and report allocation maps over Dirichlet data heterogeneity and cost sensitivity. Although evaluated on this hierarchy, the formulation can accommodate any finite candidate set. On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and a PTB-XL subset, personalization shows empirical, setting-dependent decision regimes rather than a universal benefit: higher cost sensitivity shifts Oracle mass toward the global-only depth P0; low cost sensitivity can favor deeper actions. Patterns are grid observations (three seeds per cell), not theoretical boundaries. Best-uniform is competitive with Oracle assignment (6.5 percent plus or minus 7.8 percent relative regret; 95 percent confidence interval 5.9 to 7.1), whereas random and personalize-all incur much larger regret (189.3 percent plus or minus 367.1 percent and 409.0 percent plus or minus 803.2 percent). Under the same utility, Ditto full-model personalization is substantially suboptimal once cost is counted. The contribution is an offline characterization of when personalization depth is worth its cost, not a new PFL optimizer or deployment-time scheduler. Keywords: federated learning, personalization, utility, deployment cost, allocation regime I Introduction Federated learning (FL) trains models across decentralized clients without pooling raw data. Personalized FL (PFL) adapts models to client-specific distributions through fine-tuning, regularization, representation sharing, or client-specific layers [ 10 , 11 ] . Most PFL work therefore asks how to personalize. Deployment raises a complementary question: when is personalization worth its deployment cost? Personalization consumes computation, parameters, memory, communication, and operational complexity. Personalizing every client may waste resources when the global model already suffices; a global-only policy may fail for strongly heterogeneous clients. We present a utility-based empirical decision framework for personalization-depth selection: measure predictive performance and deployment cost, form a performance–cost utility, obtain an offline Oracle reference by ex-post argmax over a finite action set, and characterize regret of practical uniform policies. Experiments instantiate 𝒜 = { P 0 , … , P 5 } \mathcal{A}=\{P_{0},\ldots,P_{5}\} and compare global-only, best-uniform, random, personalize-all, and Ditto against that Oracle. This is not a new PFL optimizer, not a deployment-time scheduler, and not a universal theory of personalization. Contributions: (i) we formulate personalization-depth selection as a finite performance–cost utility-maximization problem; (ii) we instantiate the decision space with the six-level P 0 P_{0} – P 5 P_{5} hierarchy and characterize offline Oracle assignments across heterogeneity and cost-sensitivity regimes; (iii) we quantify regret of deployable uniform policies relative to the Oracle reference and identify empirical decision regimes in which deeper personalization is or is not worth its cost; and (iv) we note that the formulation is action-space agnostic while limiting empirical claims to the evaluated P 0 P_{0} – P 5 P_{5} setting (including a PTB-XL subset and Ditto under the same utility). II Related Work II-A Classical Federated Learning FedAvg [ 1 ] learns a shared global model. FedProx [ 2 ] , SCAFFOLD [ 3 ] , FedNova [ 4 ] , and adaptive server optimization [ 5 ] address heterogeneity. Surveys document open problems and scale [ 6 , 7 ] . Non-IID effects have been measured directly [ 8 , 9 ] . II-B Personalized FL: How to Personalize The PerFedAvg method [ 10 ] uses meta-learning; Ditto [ 11 ] and pFedMe [ 12 ] regularize personalized objectives. FedPer [ 13 ] personalizes classifier heads; FedRep [ 14 ] separates representation and classifier. FedBN [ 18 ] uses local batch normalization for feature shift; FedBABU [ 15 ] decouples body and head training; APFL [ 16 ] adaptively mixes global and local models; and FedAMP [ 17 ] clusters similar clients. Adapters appear in pFedLoRA [ 19 ] , following LoRA [ 20 ] . FedALA [ 21 ] and personalization-layer decoupling [ 22 ] refine client capacity. Peer-reviewed 2025 methods continue this axis: FedFSA [ 23 ] and PFedCS [ 24 ] . Large-model personalization includes FLoRA [ 25 ] and OpenFedLLM [ 26 ] . Surveys catalogue many “how” methods [ 35 ] . Deployment cost rarely enters as an explicit shared utility over personalization depth. II-C This Work: When Personalization Is Worth Its Cost We ask under which ( task , α , λ ) (\text{task},\alpha,\lambda) client i i should personalize, and to what depth. Rather than proposing another PFL trainer or online allocator, we evaluate fixed policies, an offline Oracle reference, and Ditto under ( 2 ), map empirical decision regimes over ( α , λ ) (\alpha,\lambda) , and report regret with confidence intervals. II-D Resource-Aware FL and Benchmarks Resource-aware FL uses local SGD [ 27 ] , quantization [ 28 ] , compression [ 29 ] , and client selection such as FedCS [ 30 ] , Oort [ 31 ] , and TiFL [ 32 ] . HeteroFL [ 33 ] trains heterogeneous local capacities toward one global model; related personalized communication-efficient designs appear in industrial IoT [ 34 ] . Hardware-aware FL further couples client selection and local workload to device profiles under communication and latency constraints [ 42 ] . Benchmarks include LEAF [ 36 ] , FedScale [ 37 ] , FedML [ 38 ] , FLamby [ 39 ] , and PTB-XL [ 40 ] ; multi-institutional ECG FL has also been studied under encryption-based privacy constraints [ 41 ] . Decision Formulation. We formulate personalization-depth selection as a finite utility-maximization problem. The decision maker is a system designer, deployment planner, or FL practitioner selecting a personalization strategy under a specified performance–cost preference. The decision variable is an action a ∈ 𝒜 a\in\mathcal{A} . At λ = 0 \lambda{=}0 , the offline Oracle selects deep personalization in isolated cells. Claims about sparsity or depth must specify ( U , λ ) (U,\lambda) ; accuracy-only plots can overstate deep personalization and understate global-only efficiency when λ > 0 \lambda{>}0 . Best-uniform policy as deployment benchmark. As reported in Finding 2, the best-uniform policy is competitive across many configurations. Deployment systems should report regret against this policy before adopting heterogeneous allocation. Objectives can diverge. Ditto results illustrate that accuracy-oriented and deployment-aware utilities may favor different operating points: full-model personalization is penalized under U U when marginal Macro-F1 gain does not offset full-depth cost. Allocation maps as reporting practice. We advocate utility curves over λ \lambda , P0/deep ratios, and regret versus fixed policies with uncertainty bands—shifting from “does personalization improve accuracy?” to “under which ( task , α , λ ) (\text{task},\alpha,\lambda) is it worth its deployment cost?” Table X lists minimum reporting items. Decision formulation vs. decision policy. The framework separates decision formulation from decision policy. This study addresses the former by defining candidate actions, the utility objective, and an offline Oracle reference, and by empirically characterizing the resulting decision landscape. It does not provide a deployment-time policy that selects an action without evaluating alternatives. The characterization may support subsequent lightweight rules, calibration procedures, learned policies, or adaptive schedulers, but such mechanisms remain outside the present scope. Practical offline calibration. Exhaustive P 0 P_{0} – P 5 P_{5} evaluation is intended for offline characterization rather than routine deployment. In practice, a system designer could apply the framework during a calibration or pilot phase on representative clients, identify which actions dominate under relevant heterogeneity and cost regimes, and use the resulting evidence to define a simpler deployment policy. Recalibration may be needed if the architecture, client population, hardware, cost model, or λ \lambda range changes. Migrating from synthetic to real WFDB ECG lowered P0 ratio from 81.6% to 0.552 ± 0.167 0.552\pm 0.167 at λ = 0.3 \lambda{=}0.3 , illustrating that modality choice can shift observed regimes. Formulation-level generality vs. experiment-level scope. The same decision rule can, in principle, apply to other finite sets after redefining 𝒜 \mathcal{A} and the cost model. We therefore do not claim that observed Oracle frequencies, regret values, or regime boundaries transfer unchanged to alternative PFL methods or deployment environments. The cost model is a normalized proxy rather than real-device measurement; λ \lambda is a preference parameter, not a universally identifiable constant. The offline Oracle cannot be used directly during deployment. PTB-XL evidence is intentionally narrower than CIFAR (Lead II subset, ≤ \leq 5000 records, binary labels) and does not substitute for broader clinical evaluation. Additional limits: three seeds, simulated hardware multipliers, no native FEMNIST, one PFL comparator (Ditto), and uncorrected descriptive Wilcoxon tests. Future work includes alternative action spaces, real-device measurements, additional medical datasets, application-specific costs, and lightweight deployment policies derived from offline calibration. VIII Conclusion Personalization value in federated learning is regime-dependent rather than universal. Under U = Performance − λ ⋅ Cost U=\mathrm{Performance}-\lambda\cdot\mathrm{Cost} with default weighting and 𝒜 = { P 0 , … , P 5 } \mathcal{A}=\{P_{0},\ldots,P_{5}\} , offline Oracle depth varies with dataset, α \alpha , and λ \lambda . High λ \lambda concentrates mass on P 0 P_{0} on several vision tasks; low λ \lambda restores deeper personalization; modality shifts empirical regimes. Best-uniform remains close ( 6.5 % ± 7.8 % 6.5\%\pm 7.8\% ; CI [ 5.9 , 7.1 ] [5.9,7.1] ; 82.5% win rate); personalize-all and random do not. At λ = 0.3 \lambda{=}0.3 , mean P0 ratio 0.499 ± 0.317 0.499\pm 0.317 rejects universal global-only and universal deep-personalization laws. This work does not propose a deployment-time personalization algorithm. Instead, it formulates personalization-depth selection as a utility-based empirical decision problem and characterizes its offline decision landscape using an Oracle reference. The resulting evidence can inform future calibration rules or lightweight deployment policies, whose design and validation remain outside the present scope, including alternative PFL methods, parameter-efficient adaptation, real-device measurements, additional medical datasets, and application-specific cost functions.
